definition: Social punishment refers to using detention, torture, subjugation, and open-ended imprisonment against civilians as a way to punish and control people beyond any one individual. In the source, it is described as part of a systematic process that can begin before captivity and continue long after release, harming survivors, their families, and the wider community.

reasons: The packet supports only that torture is described as a form of social punishment in the Syrian context; it does not define the term as detention, subjugation, and open-ended imprisonment in general.
The claim that it is used to punish and control people beyond any one individual is an unsupported expansion beyond the source wording.

The source says the mechanism can begin before captivity and continue after release and can affect survivors, families, and the collective community, but it does not support the broader definitional framing given here.

The definition claims social punishment is “a way to punish and control people beyond any one individual,” but the packet does not explicitly support the “punish and control” framing or that it is specifically “beyond any one individual” (it states actions against a civilian population and impacts on “the Syrian people as a collective community,” but not this exact justification).

The definition’s list is largely supported (detain, torture, subjugate, and “indeterminate imprisonment”), and the “begins even before captivity and continues for years after release” and harms to survivors, their families, and the wider community are supported; however, the unsupported “punish and control…beyond any one individual” portion is substantive enough to fail.
